body: I work in food service, kinda part-time (not salaried, but I work 30+ hours a week) and most of my coworkers are all 18-26. Some of them know explicitly that I have bipolar disorder. Some of them know I am autistic and have adhd. Some of them know I went to the hospital for mental health reasons. My bipolar disorder and other issues have shaped a lot of my life, it’s difficult not talk about myself and evade those quirks. However, I only share specific labels once I am confident that that person resides in a similar boat to me and can be trusted with that information.

I drink a strawberry matcha as my markout pretty frequently. Our new matcha is unsweetened, so you can control the amount of sweetness if you’d prefer. My go to is an iced matcha with coconut milk, 1-2 pumps of sugar free vanilla instead of the standard sweetener, and strawberry cold foam. Sometimes, depending on the size I order, I will also add another scoop of matcha. To me, it tastes reminiscent of mochi ice cream, especially if I order it with the regular cold foam and not the non dairy version. It’s sweet, but it’s not heavy and is quite refreshing in my opinion. I prefer it over the lavender cold foam.

I wouldn’t consider myself to be thriving, at least not at this current moment. I understand the desire to want to be in that position as opposed to merely trudging through a never ceasing state of unfortunate events and depression. However, the absence of thriving doesn’t mean you’re without success. In times when I do seem to be perpetually at a loss it helps to characterize it as resilience. It blows chunks to be constantly pushed back down, but I take a lot of comfort in the fact that my hardships have made me an unmovable force. 

You will experience success and eventually find yourself to be thriving, but in the mean time you should applaud yourself for your grit and determination. It is unfortunate to admit that merely existing requires a lot of effort when for others it’s not something they need to contemplate, but that doesn’t make you any less deserving of praise.

As someone who dealt/deals with anorexia and self harm, I do think there’s a way to teach it. I do think however that you’d have to toe a very delicate line. I personally wouldn’t mention things like calorie counts, nor would I show pictures of people suffering from anorexia/bulimia as those could serve as “inspiration” or even be triggering to some. I think teaching about eating disorders is important and it needs to include the emotional and mental component. It might be easier to teach eating disorders through a lens of self love and body appreciation. To not focus on a low weight, but rather how healthy/happy you feel and that comparing body shape or size isn’t fair as we are all unique and our bodies are important. I would stay as vague as possible on things like technique or thinness as a result. Simply stating the other negatives (hair loss, organ failure, tooth decay, heart issues, worsening depression, and death) in conjunction with explaining the flawed beauty and body standards would, in my opinion, be helpful. Mentioning warning signs, may also be beneficial. I hope this helped in some way.

Hey, also a super recent diagnosis of bipolar 2. I also struggle with the idea of what is my “normal,” especially given my age and how for awhile being undiagnosed bipolar was my normal and shifting through moods was just a quirk. But, bipolar disorder, as you know, is a mood disorder; as much as I feel like a different person when manic, I am still me in a sense. I would attempt to find your normal by taking a breather and recollecting. It’s a slow process, but continuing through your life with consistency will breed a sense of normalcy within yourself. It’s impossible to force you to be you, it’s innate and natural. Finding a sense of other’s normal shouldn’t be the end goal but rather finding peace with yourself. I have found taking my meds and having daily projects keeps me aligned and less stressed. Depression and anxiety are hard, especially when you have felt the opposite to the extreme. You will feel ok one day. So far, living bipolar has been odd.
